55187012.title: File:An incomplete Medieval copper alloy bar mount dating 12th-13th century. (FindID 610567).jpg

ObjectName.value: An incomplete Medieval copper alloy bar mount dating 12th-13th century.

Categories.value: Portable Antiquities Scheme|Images uploaded by Fæ|Portable Antiquities Scheme, LON

Artist.value: Museum of London, Ben Paites, 2014-07-02 12:15:12

ImageDescription.value:
An incomplete Post Medieval copper alloy bar mount from a wick trimmer dating AD1650-1750. The mount is flat on the back and slightly convex on the front. It consists of a central rectangular panel, curving slightly at the ends and forming acorn terminals. The central panel is decorated with a series of six punched ring-and-dot motifs within a moulded linear border. The motifs are not evenly spaced. There have been several attempts to drill holes into the objects either as decoration or to form create rivet holes. One of the acorn terminals is broken at the top due to an attempt at drilling. The other terminal has a depression in the same position. Beneath these, on both terminals, are two further attempts at drilling. Each pair has a depression and a hole which breaches the edge of the object. There is a drilled hole along the edge of the central rectangular panel which does not conform to any pattern and is probably a later addition. On the back there is a pale green colouration along one edge and partially covering the rest of the surface, which may be solder or the original metal colour.

Other incomplete and fragmentary examples of wick-trimmers on the PAS database are HAMP-917D56, SOM-409575, LANCUM-B774E3, WAW-35DFC3, SWYOR-6E9078, LIN-F6A115 and PUBLIC-8BF257.

Dimensions: length: 61.21 mm; width: 11.79 mm; thickness: 2.61 mm; weight: 8.41g.

ObjectName.value: IOW-D85E28 Post-Medieval Candle Snuffer (wick trimmer)

Categories.value: Portable Antiquities Scheme|Images uploaded by Fæ|Portable Antiquities Scheme, IOW|Photographs by Frank Basford

Artist.value: The Portable Antiquities Scheme, Frank Basford, 2013-06-16 14:35:44

ImageDescription.value:
A fragment of a post-Medieval copper-alloy candle snuffer, more accurately a wick-trimmer (c. 1650-c. 1750).

The object is sub-rectangular in plan. The sides are broadley parallel and one end has a trefoil terminal. At the opposite end there is an oblique break. Each foil has a circular depression. Along the longitudinal centre-line there are two stamped ring-and-cup motifs. The remains of two copper-alloy rivets are situated at the foil end, one at each corner, although these are barely visible. The rear face is plain. The object is reddish brown with patches of a green patina on both faces. Minute flecks of silver or tin are visible at the front and also a long one edge at the rear where another element may have been attached with solder.

Length: 36.86mm; width: 13.76mm; thickness: 2.09mm. Weight: 5.25g.

Wick-trimmers would have functioned rather like a pair of scissors. Kevin Leahy comments:

'Until the invention of bending (thus self-trimming) wicks, candles needed attention to keep them in order. The box of the wick-trimmer was to catch the charred end of the wick to stop it falling onto the table cloth' (pers. comm. December 2013). The trefoil mounts from these wick-trimmers are often discovered by metal detectorists and have in the past been attributed to strap-fittings and casket mounts.

Incomplete and fragmentary wick trimmers have been recorded on The Portable Antiquities Scheme database. See finds: HAMP-917D56; LANCUM-B774E3; LIN-F6A115; PUBLIC-8BF257; SOM-409575; SWYOR-6E9078; SWYOR-CCD888 and WAW-35DFC3.

ImageDescription.value:
An incomplete Post-Medieval (1650-1750) candle snuffer, or more accurately a wick-trimmer, consisting of an open box with a flat plate forming a cover, both of which have hinged arms (now broken off byond the hinge) extending to one side.

The box is rectangular, measuring 37.83 x 29.03 x 12.55 mm externally and 31.49 x 24.25 x 9.10 mm internally. The shorter sides are angled slightly outwards as they extend upwards; the longer sides are set vertically. The longer sides are separate and soldered on; the shorter sides are bent up from the base, and one has a notch at one end to accommodate the pivoting arm for the cover.

Of the two separate longer sides, one is a decorative mount, rectangular with trefoil terminals. Each foil has a circular stamped depression, and the terminal is separated from the rest of the side by a pair of transverse grooves. Arranged horizontally between the terminals are four equidistant ring-and-dot stamps, with another pair of transverse grooves between the central two stamps. This mount measures 64.90 x 13.21 x 2.20 mm.

The other side is apparently undecorated. It has a rectangular centre, with a narrower arm projecting at one end, with a pierced V-shaped broken end holding an intact rivet which attaches it to the arm of the separate cover plate. The rivet is 3.4mm in diameter on the outside face of this arm. The arms would originally have pivoted or hinged about this rivet, and although both are now broken they would originally have ended in loop handles, as on a pair of scissors. At the other end of this side of the box, a circular-sectioned projection extends from the top corner, c.5mm in diameter and narrowing to 1.7mm diameter. It has a slight curve, possibly from damage or possibly intentional, and is c.32mm in length. The function of this projection is uncertain.

The separate hinged flat plate measures 31.83 x 24.34 x 2.35 mm. It is undecorated but has tooling marks on the underside (internal to the box). Its arm extends 16.5mm to one side and is c.8mm tall as it runs along the plate; from the end of the plate it also extends c.2mm in the opposite direction, giving a maximum height of c.10mm. This arm also has a V-shaped broken end, and the other end of the rivet which sits on the outside of this arm measures 7mm in diameter. This plate hinges down to sit inside the box, trapping the trimmed wick debris. The whole object measures (max.dimensions) 89.91 x 31.44 x 13.21 mm and weighs 54.55g.

Wick-trimmers would have functioned rather like a pair of scissors and Kevin Leahy comments "Until the invention of bending (thus self-trimming) wicks, candles needed attention to keep them in order. The box of the wick-trimmer was to catch the charred end of the wick to stop it falling onto the table cloth" (pers.comm. December 2013).

The trefoil mounts from these wick-trimmers are often discovered by metal detectorists and have in the past been attributed to strap-fittings and casket mounts. Other incomplete and fragmentary examples of wick-trimmers on the PAS database include SOM-409575, LANCUM-B774E3, WAW-35DFC3, SWYOR-6E9078, LIN-F6A115 and PUBLIC-8BF257.

ImageDescription.value: An incomplete copper alloy candle snuffer or wick trimmer dating to the post-medieval period. The surviving fragment consists of a rectangular box with crenellated reverse, and hollowed inside. There are the remains of integral projections at either long edge on one side - this would have fitted into and probably hinged to the missing elements of the trimmer. This would originally have been a swivelling joint with the missing front plate of the box which could be closed on the wick. The front edge of the plate is decorated with three ring and dot motifs. For similar more complete examples and other fragments see HAMP434, WILT-F418B3, LON-90E575, LANCUM-B774E3 and HAMP-917D56. Circa 17<sup>th</sup> - 18<sup>th</sup> century AD.

ImageDescription.value: A post-medieval copper-alloy mount, from a wick trimmer (17th/18th century). It measures 59x13.6x2.3mm and weighs 10.16g. It is missing the central projection of one of its trefoil knops. The mount is D-shaped in section, being flat to the underside with bevelled edges (flanked with a longintudinal groove) on the opposite face. This face is decorated with six ring-and-dots arranged longitudinally. The mount is divided into two sections, so each has three ring-and-dot and the two are separated by a transverse groove, which is bound on the bevelled edge by a tiny transverse rib. These also occur at the other end of each section, before the trefoil knop projects. Each trefoil knop has a hole (2.5mm diameter) in each projection, though this hole does not pierce the mount to the other side. To one side only are two rivet holes, at each end just before the trefoils. One has the rivet intact. Both have traces of solder around the holes. The reverse of the mount shows the intact rivet and the rivet hole at each corner of a ']' shape - a strip of solder, with which it was attached to the box that would have held the trimmings. There are also file marks behind one trefoil.

ImageDescription.value:
An incomplete copper-alloy strip with five in-line ring-and-dot motifs from a post-medieval wick trimmer. The broadly rectangular strip has broken at two points, each of which appear to be rivet holes; the short edges are both slightly angled at these points. The front, in addition to the ring-and-dot decoration, is bevelled along one of its long edges. The reverse is plain with evidence of solder along one of the long edges, between the rivet holes, one shorter edge perpendicular to the end of the traces along the long edge, at possibly also along the other shorter edge in a similar manner. The was where the mount was fixed to the box of the wick trimmer. The reverse is flat with a slightly incurved long edges.

Dimensions are Length 37 mm Width 12.5 mm Thickness 1.5 mm Weight 3.419g

Further examples of such mounts can be found on this database, some more ornately finished. For other examples of this kind of scissors-type candle snuffer, see WAW-35DFC3, SWYOR-6E9078, LIN-F6A115 and PUBLIC-8BF257. For a mount in place on a broken candle snuffer see HAMP-917D56 on this database.

ImageDescription.value:
Probably Post Medieval copper alloy candle trimmer fragments. The complete artefact would have resembled a pair of scissors with an upright box on one blade & a plate on the other. They are more accurately described as candle wick trimmers rather than candle snuffers. The found fragments consist of an arm on which the wick collecting box or plate was affixed, the wick collecting box itself, and the collecting box plate. The arm has piece riveted to it that has a crude zig zag decoration. This piece served either as a handle or possibly a heat guard. The elements form and method of manufacture indicate they probably pre date 1700 AD so the suggested date range is c1400 to c1700 AD.

Arm - The length is 58mm, the width is 10mm, and the thickness 7mm. Box - The length is 37mm, the width is 20mm. Plate - The length is 30mm, the width is 20mm.
The total weight is 31.7g.

see also YORYM-527572, LON-90E575
